readerTitle: Why a fully booked team makes customers wait longer
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 수리 업체, 지역 유통 창고) + 대기행렬 이론의 표준 결과 (M/M/1, Kingman 공식)
insight: 사람과 설비를 100% 가깝게 바쁘게 만드는 것은 효율이 아니라, 예상 밖의 일을 흡수할 여유를 없애 대기 시간을 폭발시키는 일이다.
misconception: 놀고 있는 시간은 낭비다. 가동률이 높을수록 일이 더 빨리, 더 많이 처리된다.

sources.text: 대기행렬 이론의 표준 결과: M/M/1 대기행렬에서 평균 대기 시간은 처리 시간 × u/(1−u)에 비례 (운영관리 교과서 공통 내용)
Kingman, J. F. C. (1961). The single server queue in heavy traffic. Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 57(4).
업체와 창고 사례 및 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 차트 수치는 M/M/1 모델의 u/(1−u) 비율로 계산하고 가동률 50%를 1로 둔 상대값입니다. 50%: 0.5/0.5 = 1, 75%: 0.75/0.25 = 3, 80%: 0.8/0.2 = 4, 90%: 0.9/0.1 = 9, 95%: 0.95/0.05 = 19. 실제 업무는 도착과 처리 시간의 변동 정도에 따라 배수가 달라지므로 카드에 'simple model'이라고 밝혔습니다.
2번 카드 정답: 75%에서 95%로 올리면 3 → 19, 약 6배(19 ÷ 3 ≈ 6.3). 카드에는 'about six times'로 적었습니다.
Kingman 공식은 대기 시간이 가동률 항 u/(1−u)과 도착·처리 시간의 변동성에 함께 비례한다는 근사식입니다. 5번 카드 설명이 이 내용과 맞는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why a fully booked team makes customers wait longer
body: A home repair company has four technicians. The owner is proud: almost every hour of their day is booked.
Yet customers now wait a week for a visit. A burst pipe on Tuesday can't be seen until Friday. Busier crews, slower service. How?

image.label: A packed technician schedule next to a long list of waiting customers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에는 빈칸 없이 꽉 찬 주간 일정표, 오른쪽에는 길게 늘어진 대기 고객 목록과 물이 새는 파이프 아이콘. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Fill the gaps in the schedule?
body: Your technicians are busy about 75% of their working day. A consultant says the gaps are waste and you should book them up to 95%.
Calls keep arriving at random, and jobs vary in length. What happens to the average customer's wait?

options.text: It stays about the same. The same crew is just doing more
options.feedback: You'd earn from more booked hours, but you'd lose the gaps that soaked up long jobs and surprise calls. Those gaps were doing real work.
Right direction. But waits don't grow in a straight line as a team gets busier. Near the top, they climb much faster.

options.text: It grows several times over, roughly six times in a simple model
options.feedback: Yes. Going from 75% to 95% busy can multiply waits many times when work arrives unevenly. The next card shows the curve.

cards.title: Waits explode near 100%.
body: In a simple queueing model, average wait grows with *busy ÷ idle*. At 50% busy, call the wait 1. Each step toward full looks small. The wait does not.

groups.label: Relative wait by how busy the team is

cards.callout: From 90% to 95% busy, the wait roughly doubles.

image.label: Waits explode near 100%.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: The utilization trap
body: **Utilization** is the share of time a person or machine is busy. The **utilization trap** is treating high utilization as the goal, when the customer cares about speed.
When work arrives unevenly, idle time is not waste. It is the buffer that absorbs surprises. Remove it, and every surprise turns into a delay for everyone behind it.

cards.title: Delays pile up and never get paid back.
body: One job runs an hour long. Two emergency calls land at once. With some slack, the crew catches up by afternoon.
At 95% busy, there is no afternoon gap. The delay rolls into tomorrow, then the next day. A team that is almost always busy rarely gets the chance to clear its backlog.
Queueing research says waits depend on two things: **how busy you are** and how much the work varies. The more uneven the work, the earlier the curve turns steep.

image.label: Two schedules: one with gaps absorbing a long job, one without
image.brief: 두 개의 하루 일정 막대 비교. 위쪽은 중간중간 빈칸이 있어 길어진 작업이 빈칸에 흡수됨. 아래쪽은 빈칸이 없어 길어진 작업이 뒤의 작업을 모두 밀어내고 다음 날로 넘어가는 화살표.

cards.title: The same trap in other places
list: **Accounting firms in tax season:** fully booked staff mean one tricky client delays a dozen others
**Hospital beds:** wards run near full have no room for the next ambulance
**Delivery fleets:** every truck on the road means one breakdown cancels a route
cards.callout: Wherever work arrives at random, full means slow.
cards.softwareNote: Servers running near full capacity respond slowly long before they crash. An engineering team booked solid on planned work can't fix an urgent bug without delaying everything else.

cards.title: Slack has a cost, and not every place needs it.
body: Idle hours still cost wages and equipment. The trap matters most when work arrives unpredictably and waiting is costly, like emergency repairs or same-day orders.
If work is steady and can wait, such as a factory line with a planned backlog, running close to full can be fine.
So don't aim for a utilization number. Watch what customers feel, like wait time or on-time delivery, and keep only as much slack as that requires.

cards.title: Now it's a distribution warehouse.
body: Your regional warehouse promises same-day shipping to shops. Packers are busy 92% of the time on average, but orders spike on Mondays. Late shipments are rising.

options.text: Cut one packer. On quieter days some stand idle
options.feedback: You save one wage but push the team even closer to full. Monday delays would grow sharply and more shops would get late orders.

options.text: Add flexible help for Mondays and track on-time shipping, not packer busyness
options.feedback: You pay for extra hours only when the spike hits, and you measure what shops actually care about. Average utilization drops a little, and that's the point.

options.text: Ask packers to work overtime every Monday
options.feedback: It adds capacity at the right time, but tired staff make more errors and the team still has no room for surprises.

cards.title: A little idle time keeps the whole system fast.
body: When work arrives unevenly, pushing people toward 100% busy makes customers wait far longer. Manage for speed, not busyness.
**Try it today:** pick one team or machine. Estimate how busy it is, then check how long customers wait for it. If it's above 85% busy and waits are growing, you may be in the trap.
